title: How Long Does It Take to Sober Up? Hours-Per-Drink Math
excerpt: How long it really takes to sober up: the hours-per-drink math, a chart by number of drinks, why coffee and cold showers don't work, and when it's safe to drive.
metaDescription: How long does it take to sober up? The hours-per-drink math, a chart for 1 to 8+ drinks, what doesn't work (coffee, showers), and when it's safe to drive.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed pace, and nothing you can buy or do speeds it up in a meaningful way. On average, blood alcohol falls by about 0.015 percentage points per hour, which works out to roughly one standard drink per hour for an average adult. So if you had five drinks, plan on something like five to seven hours from your last drink before your blood alcohol is back near zero, and longer if you drank fast, are smaller, or had stronger pours than you think. Coffee, cold showers, food after the fact, and sleep do not change that clock. Time is the only thing that sobers you up.

**The quick rules:** Count your drinks in standard drinks, not glasses. Expect about one hour per standard drink, counted from when you started, as a rough floor rather than a promise. Add extra time if you drank quickly, on an empty stomach, or had cocktails, craft beer, or big wine pours. If you are thinking about driving, don't use this math to decide. Plan another way home. "Feeling fine" is not a reliable test.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research on how the body processes alcohol. It cannot tell you your exact blood alcohol level or whether you are safe to drive. **Get help right away (call 911 in the US) if** someone who has been drinking is confused and can't be woken or kept awake, is vomiting while very drowsy, has slow or irregular breathing (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute or long pauses), has blue-tinged or pale, cold skin, or has a seizure. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, and "letting them sleep it off" can be fatal. Do not leave them alone, and lay them on their side if they are lying down.

## How Long Does It Take to Sober Up? The Short Math

Your body gets rid of alcohol mostly through your liver, and the liver works at a steady rate no matter how much is waiting in line. That's why "sobering up" is really a waiting game.

The number most researchers and public health sources use is an elimination rate of about **0.015 g/dL per hour**. In plain words: if your blood alcohol concentration (BAC) is 0.08% right now, it will drop to about 0.065% an hour from now, about 0.05% after two hours, and so on. Real people vary. Studies of elimination rates usually find most adults somewhere between about 0.010 and 0.020 per hour, with regular heavy drinkers sometimes clearing a little faster because their livers have adapted.

Here is what that average rate means in hours:

| Your BAC at the moment you stop drinking | Approximate time to reach zero |
|---|---|
| 0.02% (one drink, feeling it slightly) | About 1 to 1.5 hours |
| 0.05% (noticeably buzzed) | About 3 to 3.5 hours |
| 0.08% (US legal driving limit) | About 5 to 5.5 hours |
| 0.10% | About 6.5 to 7 hours |
| 0.15% (clearly drunk) | About 10 hours |
| 0.20% (very drunk, at risk of blackout) | About 13 hours |

These numbers assume the average rate. If you are a slow eliminator, add a few hours to the higher rows. And remember the starting point is your BAC when you stop drinking, which you usually don't know. That's the biggest weakness of any sober-up timer, including the one in your head.

If you want a quick estimate based on your weight, sex, and drinks, our [blood alcohol calculator guide](/never-hungover/blood-alcohol-calculator) walks through it. For what the BAC numbers themselves mean, see [what is BAC](/never-hungover/what-is-bac).

## What Counts as "One Drink"?

The one-drink-per-hour rule only works if you count drinks the way researchers do. In the US, a **standard drink** contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol. That's roughly:

- 12 ounces of regular beer at about 5% alcohol
- 5 ounces of wine at about 12% alcohol
- 1.5 ounces (one shot) of 80-proof liquor at 40% alcohol

The problem is that real drinks are rarely standard:

- **A pint of IPA at 7% is about 1.6 standard drinks.** A 16-ounce can of 8% craft beer is closer to 2.
- **A restaurant wine pour is often 6 to 9 ounces,** which is 1.2 to nearly 2 standard drinks. A third of a bottle of wine is about 2 standard drinks.
- **Cocktails often contain two or more shots.** A Long Island iced tea, a large margarita, or a strong home-poured mixed drink can easily be 2 to 3 standard drinks in one glass.
- **Hard seltzers and canned cocktails vary** from about 4% to over 8%, so read the can.

If you had "four drinks" but they were pints of strong beer or generous cocktails, you may have had six or seven standard drinks. Your sober-up time should be based on that number, not the glass count.

## How Long to Sober Up After 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or More Drinks

People mostly want a number for their own night. Here's a rough guide based on standard drinks, the average elimination rate, and typical body sizes. Treat the low end as a minimum and the high end as more realistic for smaller people, women, fast drinking, or an empty stomach.

| Standard drinks | Rough time until BAC is near zero (from your first drink) |
|---|---|
| 1 | About 1 to 2 hours |
| 2 | About 2 to 4 hours |
| 3 | About 3 to 5 hours |
| 4 | About 4 to 7 hours |
| 5 | About 5 to 8 hours |
| 6 to 7 | About 7 to 11 hours |
| 8 or more | 10 hours or longer, often into the next afternoon |

A few things to notice:

- **The clock starts when you start, but drinking faster than about one drink an hour stacks up alcohol.** If you have four drinks in one hour, your BAC climbs much higher than if you spread them over four hours, and you'll be waiting longer after your last sip.
- **Your BAC keeps rising after your last drink.** Alcohol takes time to absorb. Peak BAC usually arrives 30 to 90 minutes after you stop, depending on food and how fast you drank. So the drive home right after "last call" can be at a higher BAC than you had while sitting at the bar.
- **Heavier drinking pushes clearance into the next day.** After eight or more drinks, many people still have measurable alcohol in their blood the next morning, even after a full night's sleep.

### Worked example: a 180-pound man

Say a 180-pound man has five standard drinks over three hours, with dinner. A common estimate (the Widmark formula, a decades-old method still used in forensic work) puts his peak BAC somewhere around 0.07% to 0.09% after accounting for some elimination during those three hours. At 0.015 per hour, it takes about five to six more hours to reach zero. If he stopped at 11 p.m., he'd likely be near zero around 4 or 5 a.m.

### Worked example: a 135-pound woman

Now a 135-pound woman has the same five drinks over the same three hours. Because she has less body water for the alcohol to spread into, her peak is likely much higher, often around 0.14% to 0.17%. At the same elimination rate, that's roughly 9 to 11 more hours. If she stopped at 11 p.m., she might not be near zero until 8 to 10 a.m.

Same drinks, same night, a very different morning. These are rough illustrations, not personal readings, but they show why "I'll be fine in a few hours" goes wrong so often.

## Why Some People Take Longer to Sober Up

The elimination rate is fairly steady, but how high your BAC climbs in the first place varies a lot. Higher peak, longer wait. The main factors:

- **Body size and body water.** Alcohol spreads through the water in your body. A larger person has more water to dilute it, so the same drink produces a lower BAC.
- **Sex.** On average, women have a lower proportion of body water than men of the same weight, and some research suggests differences in stomach alcohol metabolism too. Women generally reach a higher BAC from the same number of drinks.
- **Food.** Eating before or while drinking slows the rate alcohol leaves your stomach and reaches your bloodstream. That lowers your peak and can shorten how long you're impaired. Food eaten *after* you've finished drinking does very little for the alcohol already in your blood.
- **Speed of drinking.** Shots and fast rounds spike your BAC. Sipping one drink an hour keeps it lower.
- **Drink type.** Carbonated drinks (champagne, mixers with soda) may be absorbed slightly faster. Strong drinks just carry more alcohol per glass.
- **Genetics.** Variants in the enzymes that break down alcohol (alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase) affect how people respond to alcohol. Some, common in people of East Asian descent, cause facial flushing and a buildup of a toxic by-product called acetaldehyde. These variants matter more for how you feel than for how quickly BAC drops.
- **Medications and health.** Liver disease can slow clearance. Some medicines interact with alcohol or add to its sedating effects. If you take regular medication, ask a pharmacist how it combines with alcohol.

For more on the enzymes and why individual rates differ, see [how to speed up alcohol metabolism](/never-hungover/how-to-speed-up-alcohol-metabolism), which looks honestly at what can and can't change the rate.

## How to Sober Up Fast: What Actually Works (and What Doesn't)

This is the part where most people hope for a trick. There isn't one. Your liver processes alcohol mainly with an enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase, which works at close to full capacity once you've had a couple of drinks. You can't make it work much faster by adding anything to the system.

Here's how the popular methods hold up.

### Coffee: makes you more alert, not more sober

Caffeine can make you feel less sleepy, but it does not lower your BAC. Research on mixing caffeine and alcohol suggests the main effect is that people *feel* less impaired than they are, which can lead to riskier choices, like driving or drinking more. A "wide-awake drunk" is still drunk. Coffee after drinking is fine for a groggy morning, but it is not a sobering tool.

### Cold showers: a shock, not a cure

A cold shower may jolt you awake for a few minutes. It doesn't touch the alcohol in your blood. It can also be risky if you're unsteady on your feet, since slips in the shower are a real danger when you're drunk.

### Water: good idea, wrong reason

Drinking water won't flush alcohol out faster in any meaningful way. Only a few percent of alcohol leaves through urine, breath, and sweat combined. But water does help with the dehydration that alcohol causes, and alternating water with drinks slows down how much alcohol you take in. That makes it one of the best habits for the night and the morning, just not a sobering-up hack. See [does water help a hangover](/never-hungover/does-water-help-a-hangover) for more.

### Food: helps before, not much after

Eating before and during drinking genuinely lowers your peak BAC. Eating after you've finished does little for the alcohol that's already absorbed. A late-night meal might settle your stomach, but it won't sober you up.

### Exercise and sweating it out

You lose only a tiny share of alcohol through sweat and breath. A jog, a sauna, or a hot bath won't change your BAC much, and the sauna or hot bath can be dangerous because alcohol already lowers blood pressure and impairs judgment. Skip it.

### Vomiting

Throwing up only removes alcohol that's still in your stomach and hasn't been absorbed yet. Once you're feeling drunk, most of it is already in your blood. Making yourself vomit adds dehydration and choking risk without helping much. If someone is vomiting repeatedly while confused or very drowsy, that's a warning sign of alcohol poisoning, not a sign they're "getting it out."

### Sleep

Sleep does not speed up alcohol elimination. It just passes the time while your liver does its work, which is the one thing that actually helps. That's why people often feel "sobered up" after sleeping. Two cautions: alcohol makes sleep lighter and more broken in the second half of the night, and someone who is very drunk should not be left alone to sleep it off on their back.

### Sugar, fructose, and "sober up" drinks

There's some old research suggesting fructose (fruit sugar) may slightly increase the rate of alcohol metabolism in some people, but the effect is small and inconsistent, and not something to rely on. Products sold as "sober up" or "alcohol detox" drinks don't have good evidence behind them for lowering BAC. There is no good evidence that any over-the-counter product will make you safe to drive sooner.

**The bottom line on speed:** the only things that reliably lower the BAC you'll need to wait out are drinking less, drinking slower, and eating beforehand. Once alcohol is in your blood, waiting is the method.

## Can You Sober Up in 1 Hour?

No, not from real drinking. In one hour, an average person's BAC drops by about 0.015%. If you're at 0.10%, an hour later you're still around 0.085%, which is over the US legal driving limit and still impaired. You might *feel* a bit better after an hour, especially if your BAC has peaked and started to fall. Many people feel more sober on the way down than they did at the same BAC on the way up, which is a well-known effect in alcohol research. That feeling is unreliable.

If you've had only one standard drink, with food, over an hour or more, you may be close to baseline within an hour or two. Beyond that, one hour won't do it.

## How Long Until You Can Drive?

This is the most important version of the question, and the honest answer is that no chart can tell you when you, specifically, are safe to drive.

A few facts to keep in mind:

- **Impairment starts well below the legal limit.** Driving skills like divided attention, reaction time, and judging distance begin to slip at BAC levels of around 0.02% to 0.05%. The US limit of 0.08% (0.05% in Utah) is a legal line, not a safety line. Many countries use 0.05% or lower.
- **Your BAC can still be rising after you stop.** Driving 30 minutes after your last drink may put you at your peak.
- **"I feel fine" is not evidence.** Alcohol impairs your ability to judge your own impairment.
- **Morning-after driving catches people.** After a heavy night, it's common to be over the limit the next morning, especially if you stopped drinking late. Working out the example above: someone who reached 0.16% at 1 a.m. may not reach zero until around noon.
- **Consumer breathalyzers help, but aren't perfect.** Cheap devices can be off, especially if you've recently had a drink or used mouthwash. Treat a reading as a rough guide, not permission.

The safest plan is to decide before you drink: designated driver, rideshare, public transit, or staying put. If you're unsure, don't drive. If you'd like to understand how long alcohol stays detectable in breath and blood tests, see [how long does alcohol stay in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system).

## Sober vs. Hangover: Why You Can Feel Worse After Your BAC Hits Zero

Being sober and feeling okay are not the same thing. Research on hangovers suggests symptoms tend to be worst around the time your BAC returns to zero, often the next morning. By then the alcohol is gone, but its after-effects are not: poor sleep, dehydration, irritation of the stomach lining, inflammation, low blood sugar in some people, and leftover acetaldehyde.

So when you wake up at 9 a.m. after a big night, you may be:

- **Still over zero BAC**, if you drank heavily or late, and
- **Hungover at the same time**, or both one after the other.

A hangover usually lasts most of a day and can stretch to around 24 hours after heavy drinking. Our guide on [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) covers what to expect and what helps.

## How to Get Through the Wait Safely

If you've had too much and just need to let time pass, here's a sensible routine:

1. **Stop drinking.** Obvious, but the most important step. Every extra drink adds roughly another hour.
2. **Switch to water** or an electrolyte drink, sipping rather than chugging if you feel queasy.
3. **Eat something light** if you can, like toast, crackers, or a banana. It won't sober you up, but it can settle your stomach.
4. **Stay with friends** and make sure someone knows how you're getting home.
5. **Don't drive, swim, bike, or climb anything.** Impaired balance and judgment cause many alcohol-related injuries.
6. **Skip sleep aids and sedating medicines.** Antihistamines like diphenhydramine and other sedatives add to alcohol's effect on breathing and alertness.
7. **Lie on your side if you feel the room spinning,** with one foot on the floor if that helps. More on that in our guide to [the drunk spins](/never-hungover/drunk-spins).
8. **Set an alarm and plan your morning.** If you need to drive early, arrange a ride or another way to get there now, rather than counting on how you feel in the morning.

If you're looking after a friend who is very drunk, keep them on their side, check on them regularly, and don't let them "sleep it off" alone if they're hard to wake.

## When to See a Doctor or Call for Help

Most nights of social drinking end with nothing worse than a rough morning. But alcohol poisoning is real, and it often happens when someone drinks a lot quickly, such as shots, drinking games, or chugging.

**Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone who has been drinking:**

- Is confused, can't stay awake, or can't be woken up
- Has slow or irregular breathing, or long pauses between breaths
- Is vomiting while passed out or very drowsy
- Has a seizure
- Has pale, bluish, or cold, clammy skin
- Has a very low body temperature

Don't wait for every sign to appear. Don't give them coffee or put them in a cold shower, and don't assume they'll be fine by morning. BAC can keep rising for a while after they stop drinking, even while they're asleep. Our guide on [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) explains what to do while you wait for help.

**See a doctor (not an emergency) if:**

- You regularly need many hours to feel normal after what seem like modest amounts of alcohol
- You have yellowing of your skin or eyes, or pain under your right ribs
- You notice shaking, sweating, anxiety, or a racing heart when you go a day or two without drinking. These can be early withdrawal signs, and it's worth talking to a doctor plainly about them, since stopping suddenly after heavy daily drinking can be dangerous without medical support.

## Can a Supplement Help You Sober Up?

People often ask whether DHM (dihydromyricetin), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, can sober you up. Here's the honest picture.

The best-known study, published in the *Journal of Neuroscience* in 2012, found that DHM reduced signs of alcohol intoxication in rats and appeared to act on the same brain receptors (GABA-A receptors) that alcohol affects. Lab and animal studies have also looked at its effects on alcohol-processing enzymes in the liver. That's interesting research, but it's mostly in animals, and human data are limited.

There is no good evidence that DHM lowers your BAC in a way that makes you safe to drive, and you should never use it, or any supplement, as a reason to drive or keep drinking. Where some people find it useful is as part of a routine for feeling better the next morning, alongside water, food, sleep, and fewer drinks. If you want to try it, two widely used options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

The most reliable way to spend less time waiting to sober up is to need less time in the first place. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence: pacing, eating first, water between drinks, and knowing what's in your glass.

## The Bottom Line

- Your body clears alcohol at roughly 0.015% BAC per hour, about one standard drink per hour for an average adult. Nothing you can do reliably speeds that up.
- Count standard drinks honestly. Strong beers, big wine pours, and cocktails often hold 1.5 to 3 standard drinks each.
- After five drinks, think five to eight hours. After eight or more, expect alcohol in your blood the next morning.
- Coffee, cold showers, food after drinking, exercise, and sleep don't lower your BAC. Time does.
- Feeling sober isn't the same as being sober, and being sober isn't the same as being safe to drive. When in doubt, don't drive.
- Signs of alcohol poisoning, like confusion, slow breathing, or someone who can't be woken, need emergency help right away.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How long does it take to sober up after drinking?**

On average, your body lowers blood alcohol by about 0.015% per hour, roughly one standard drink per hour. A night of four or five standard drinks usually takes about five to eight hours from your first drink to get close to zero, and heavier drinking can take 10 hours or more. Smaller people, women, fast drinking, and drinking on an empty stomach all push the time longer.

**How can I sober up fast?**

You can't meaningfully speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol. Coffee, cold showers, exercise, and food after drinking may make you feel more alert, but they don't lower your BAC. What helps is stopping drinking, switching to water, and waiting. To spend less time impaired next time, eat beforehand, drink slower, and have fewer drinks.

**Can you sober up in an hour?**

Not from more than about one drink. An hour lowers your BAC by roughly 0.015%, so someone at 0.10% would still be around 0.085% an hour later, over the US driving limit. You might feel a little better as your BAC starts to fall, but that feeling isn't a reliable sign you're sober.

**Does coffee sober you up?**

No. Caffeine can make you feel more awake, but it doesn't lower the amount of alcohol in your blood. Research suggests mixing caffeine and alcohol can make people underestimate how impaired they are, which can lead to risky choices like driving. Coffee is fine for a groggy morning, but it is not a way to sober up.

**How long after drinking can I drive?**

No chart can tell you exactly when you're safe to drive, because your starting BAC and elimination rate are unknown. As a rough guide, allow at least one hour per standard drink, counted from your first drink, and add extra time for strong drinks, fast drinking, or an empty stomach. Driving skills start to slip well below the 0.08% legal limit. If you've been drinking heavily or aren't sure, don't drive, and be careful about driving the next morning.

**Does sleeping sober you up faster?**

No. Sleep doesn't speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol. It just lets time pass while your body does its work. After a heavy night you can still have alcohol in your blood when you wake up. Someone who is very drunk and hard to wake shouldn't be left alone to sleep it off, because that can be a sign of alcohol poisoning.

**Why do I still feel drunk the next morning?**

If you drank heavily or late, you may still have alcohol in your blood the next morning, since it can take 10 hours or more to clear. Even once your BAC reaches zero, hangover symptoms like headache, fatigue, and poor concentration often peak around that point. Being sober and feeling normal can be several hours apart.

**Do women take longer to sober up than men?**

Women usually reach a higher BAC from the same number of drinks because, on average, they have less body water for alcohol to spread into. The rate the body clears alcohol is broadly similar, but starting from a higher peak means it takes longer to get back to zero.

**Does DHM help you sober up?**

There's no good evidence that DHM lowers blood alcohol in people in a way that makes you sober or safe to drive. Animal research, including a 2012 rat study, found it reduced signs of intoxication, but human data are limited. Some people use it as part of their next-morning routine, but it should never be a reason to drive or keep drinking.
